resources.title: 01. Atomic Theory
resources.content: COURSE: CHM 101 \| LEVEL: 100L --- ## 📌 Learning Objectives 1. State Dalton's five assumptions and explain why his model mattered. 2. Explain the three foundational laws of chemical combination and how they connect to Dalton's theory. 3. Describe why Dalton's "solid sphere" model eventually broke down. 4. Place the key discoveries (electron, nucleus, neutron) in correct chronological order. --- ## 🔑 Key Concepts This topic answers a deceptively simple question: what is matter actually made of, at the smallest scale? Everything physical is built from atoms — tiny particles that bond together to form molecules. Atomic theory is the story of scientists progressively discovering that atoms, first assumed to be simple indivisible spheres, are actually made of smaller charged particles arranged in a specific structure — and that structure determines everything about an element's chemistry. --- ## 📖 Detailed Notes ### Section 1: What Is Matter? Matter is anything that occupies space and has mass — obvious matter (water, wood, steel) and less obvious matter (air, dust) are both built from atoms. ### Section 2: Dalton's Atomic Theory John Dalton proposed the first real scientific atomic model, resting on five assumptions: 1. All matter is made of atoms — solid, indivisible spheres. 2. Atoms are indestructible and unchangeable — can't be created, destroyed, split, or converted between elements. 3. Atoms of the same element are identical to each other, but different from atoms of any other element. 4. Atoms combine in small whole-number ratios during chemical reactions. 5. Elements can combine in more than one ratio — explaining why carbon and oxygen form both CO and CO₂. Why this mattered: Dalton was the first to explain chemical behavior using discrete particles, rather than treating matter as infinitely divisible. ### Section 3: The Three Foundational Laws These laws were observed before Dalton's theory — his model was built partly to explain them. - Law of Conservation of Mass (Lavoisier): in a closed system, mass is neither created nor destroyed during a reaction. - Law of Definite Proportions (Proust): a compound always contains its elements in a fixed mass ratio, regardless of how or where it was made. Water is always \~11% hydrogen, \~89% oxygen by mass — every time. - Law of Multiple Proportions: when two elements form more than one compound, the masses of one element combining with a fixed mass of the other appear in small whole-number ratios. Dalton's whole-number-ratio assumptions (#4, #5) are essentially his theoretical explanation for why the Law of Multiple Proportions holds true. ### Section 4: Why Dalton's Model Broke Down About 50 years after Dalton, evidence accumulated (roughly 1890s–1930s) that atoms are NOT solid, indivisible spheres. Two research threads drove this: 1. Research into the electrical nature of matter — leading to the discovery that atoms contain smaller charged particles. 2. Research into how matter interacts with energy — leading to understanding how those particles are arranged inside the atom. Conclusion: atoms are divisible, built from subatomic particles — the proton, neutron, and electron. ### Section 5: Timeline — Building the Modern Atomic Model | Year | Scientist | Contribution | | --- | --- | --- | | 1897 | J.J. Thomson | Discovered the electron (Cathode Ray Experiment) | | 1909 | Ernest Rutherford | Proposed the nuclear atom | | 1913 | Henry Moseley | Determined atomic number as an element's true identity | | 1913 | Niels Bohr | Bohr model — electrons in fixed orbits | | 1921 | Bohr–Bury | Scheme for electronic arrangement | | 1926 | Erwin Schrödinger | Wave equation — "electron cloud" model | | 1932 | James Chadwick | Discovered the neutron | --- ## 🎯 Clinical/Real-World Applications - Every drug's chemical behavior traces back to electron arrangement — this topic is the true foundation underneath biochemistry and pharmacology. - Radioisotopes used in medical imaging and cancer treatment only make sense once you understand atoms have a nucleus that can be unstable. - Atomic number is how every element — and every drug, mineral, biomolecule — is identified and organized. --- ## ⚠️ Common Mistakes - Thinking Dalton's model is still fully accurate — atoms ARE divisible. - Mixing up discovery order: Thomson (1897) → Rutherford (1909) → Chadwick (1932). - Confusing Definite Proportions (one compound, fixed ratio) with Multiple Proportions (two elements, multiple compounds, whole-number ratios). --- ## 📝 Quick Revision Summary - Dalton: atoms = solid, indivisible, identical within an element, whole-number combining ratios. - Three laws: Conservation of Mass, Definite Proportions, Multiple Proportions. - Discovery order: Thomson's electron (1897) → Rutherford's nucleus (1909) → Bohr's orbits (1913) → Chadwick's neutron (1932). --- ## ✅ Self-Test Checklist - [Remember] State Dalton's five assumptions in your own words. - [Understand] Which law explains why water is always H₂O, never H₃O? - [Remember] Order: Chadwick's neutron, Thomson's electron, Rutherford's nuclear atom. - [Analyse] Why did Dalton's "solid sphere" model eventually fail? --- Next: Thermochemistry →

resources.title: 02. Thermochemistry
resources.content: COURSE: CHM 101 \| LEVEL: 100L --- ## 📌 Learning Objectives 1. Calculate enthalpy of reaction from formation enthalpies, correctly applying stoichiometric coefficients. 2. Calculate entropy change and convert units correctly. 3. Apply the Gibbs Free Energy equation to determine whether a reaction is spontaneous. 4. Identify which of the three core calculations (enthalpy, entropy, spontaneity) a problem needs. --- ## 🔑 Key Concepts Thermochemistry answers three connected questions: how much heat does a reaction release/absorb (enthalpy)? How does its disorder change (entropy)? Will it happen on its own (spontaneity)? Almost every problem reduces to one of exactly three calculations. --- ## 📖 Detailed Notes ### Section 1: Internal Energy (U) ΔU = ΔKE + ΔPE, also ΔU = ΔH − ΔW. U is a state function — depends only on start/end points, not the path. ### Section 2: Enthalpy (H) ΔH° = ΣH(products) − ΣH(reactants) Two rules to lock in: - Enthalpy of formation of an element in standard state = zero. - Always multiply by stoichiometric mole coefficients — the #1 place marks are lost. Worked Example: 2CO(g) + O₂(g) → 2CO₂(g) ΔH°f(CO)=−110.4, ΔH°f(CO₂)=−393, ΔH°f(O₂)=0 ```javascript ΔH°rxn = [2×(−393)] − [2×(−110.4)+0] = −786 − (−220.8) = −565.2 kJ ``` ### Section 3: Entropy (S) ΔS = ΔH/T. State function: ΔS = ΣS(products) − ΣS(reactants). Unit: J K⁻¹. Exam trap: convert units (kJ vs J) to match before combining in Gibbs equation. Worked Example: 1 mol water absorbs 40,700 J at 383K → ΔS = 40700/383 ≈ 106.26 J K⁻¹ ### Section 4: Gibbs Free Energy (G) ΔG = ΔH − TΔS - ΔG \< 0 → spontaneous - ΔG > 0 → non-spontaneous Worked Example: ΔH=+90kJ/mol, ΔS=0.012kJ/K, T=308K ΔG = 90 − (308×0.012) = 90 − 3.696 = +86.304 kJ/mol → non-spontaneous ### Section 5: Identifying Which Calculation a Question Needs 1. Enthalpy? → ΔH = ΣH(products)−ΣH(reactants) 2. Entropy? → ΔS = ΔH/T 3. Spontaneity? → ΔG = ΔH−TΔS, check sign --- ## 🎯 Clinical/Real-World Applications - ATP hydrolysis (body's energy currency) is a ΔG\<0 spontaneous reaction — foundational to biochemistry. - Enzyme optimal temperature ranges relate directly to entropy/enthalpy shifts. - Drug stability/shelf life depends on whether degradation is thermodynamically favorable at storage temp. --- ## ⚠️ Common Mistakes - Forgetting stoichiometric coefficients in ΔH°rxn calculations. - Mixing kJ/J units between enthalpy and entropy. - Assuming positive ΔH = automatically non-spontaneous (it's ΔG's sign that matters, not ΔH alone). - Confusing "spontaneous" with "fast" (that's kinetics, a separate topic). --- ## 📝 Quick Revision Summary - ΔH°rxn = ΣH(products)−ΣH(reactants); elements=0; apply coefficients. - ΔS = ΔH/T; watch unit conversions. - ΔG = ΔH−TΔS; ΔG\<0=spontaneous. --- ## ✅ Self-Test Checklist - [Remember] Why is an element's enthalpy of formation always zero? - [Apply] Given ΔH and ΔU at constant pressure, solve for ΔW. - [Apply] Given ΔH and ΔS at a temperature, determine spontaneity. - [Analyse] What's the most common entropy unit-conversion mistake? --- Next: Chemical Kinetics →

resources.title: 03. Chemical Kinetics
resources.content: COURSE: CHM 101 \| LEVEL: 100L --- ## 📌 Learning Objectives 1. Define reaction rate and express it correctly using stoichiometry. 2. Write and interpret a rate law; determine reaction order from experimental data. 3. Apply integrated rate laws for first- and second-order reactions, including half-life. 4. Use the Arrhenius equation to relate temperature, activation energy, and rate constant. --- ## 🔑 Key Concepts Kinetics studies how fast a reaction happens. Three big ideas: rate law (experimental, not read off the equation), integrated rate laws (predict concentration at any time), Arrhenius equation (why rate increases with temperature). --- ## 📖 Detailed Notes ### Section 1: Reaction Rate and Stoichiometry Rate = −Δ\[A\]/Δt (reactants) or +Δ\[B\]/Δt (products). To compare species fairly: Rate = −(1/a)(Δ\[A\]/Δt) = −(1/b)(Δ\[B\]/Δt) = (1/c)(Δ\[C\]/Δt) = (1/d)(Δ\[D\]/Δt) ### Section 2: Rate Law and Reaction Order Rate = k\[A\]ˣ\[B\]ʸ — x and y are experimentally determined, NOT the stoichiometric coefficients. Overall order = x+y. Method of Initial Rates: compare runs where only one concentration changed; take rate ratios to isolate each order. ### Section 3: Integrated Rate Laws First order: ln(\[A\]/\[A\]₀) = −kt. Plot ln\[A\] vs t → straight line = first order. Second order: 1/\[A\] = kt + 1/\[A\]₀. Plot 1/\[A\] vs t → straight line = second order. Half-life: - First order: t½ = 0.693/k (concentration-independent) - Second order: t½ = 1/(k\[A\]₀) (concentration-DEPENDENT) ### Section 4: The Arrhenius Equation k = A·e\^(−Ea/RT) Linearized: ln k = −(Ea/R)(1/T) + ln A Two-temperature: ln(k₂/k₁) = (Ea/R)\[(1/T₁) − (1/T₂)\] Rule of thumb: \~10°C rise ≈ doubles rate constant. --- ## 🎯 Clinical/Real-World Applications - Drug metabolism/half-life follows the same first-order math — directly relevant to pharmacology. - Enzyme kinetics: enzymes lower activation energy to sustain life at body temperature. - Fever measurably shifts enzymatic reaction rates throughout the body (Arrhenius logic). --- ## ⚠️ Common Mistakes - Assuming reaction order = stoichiometric coefficients (it doesn't). - Using first-order half-life formula for second-order reactions. - Forgetting to divide by stoichiometric coefficients when comparing rates. - Mixing up which plot (ln\[A\] vs 1/\[A\]) tests which order. --- ## 📝 Quick Revision Summary - Rate law: experimental orders, not from the equation. - First order: ln\[A\] vs t linear; t½=0.693/k. Second order: 1/\[A\] vs t linear; t½ depends on \[A\]₀. - Arrhenius: k=A·e\^(−Ea/RT); \~10°C rise doubles k. --- ## ✅ Self-Test Checklist - [Remember] State reaction rate definition and stoichiometry-corrected expression. - [Apply] Use method of initial rates to determine a rate law. - [Apply] Calculate fraction remaining given a first-order half-life. - [Analyse] Determine reaction order from concentration-vs-time data. - [Apply] Calculate Ea from rate constants at two temperatures. --- Next: Chemical Equilibria →

resources.title: 04. Chemical Equilibria
resources.content: COURSE: CHM 101 \| LEVEL: 100L --- ## 📌 Learning Objectives 1. Explain equilibrium at the molecular level; write correct K expressions. 2. Manipulate K when a reaction is reversed or scaled. 3. Use ICE tables to solve for equilibrium concentrations. 4. Apply Q and Le Chatelier's Principle to predict shifts. --- ## 🔑 Key Concepts Equilibrium does NOT mean the reaction stopped — forward and reverse rates are equal. Three tools: K (where balance sits), ICE tables (calculating concentrations), Le Chatelier's Principle (predicting shifts). --- ## 📖 Detailed Notes ### Section 1: Writing K Rule: aqueous + gas species appear; solvents/solids do not. N₂(g)+3H₂(g)⇌2NH₃(g) → K=\[NH₃\]²/(\[N₂\]\[H₂\]³) K>>1 = product-favored. K\<\<1 = reactant-favored. ### Section 2: Manipulating K - Reverse: K(rev) = 1/K(fwd) - Scale by n: K(new) = K(orig)ⁿ ### Section 3: ICE Tables Initial, Change, Equilibrium — Change row MUST respect stoichiometric coefficients (coefficient of 2 = ±2x, not ±x). ### Section 4: Q vs K Same formula, different timing. Q\K → shifts backward. Q=K → at equilibrium. ### Section 5: Le Chatelier's Principle Concentration: add → shifts away; remove → shifts toward. Temperature: exothermic+heat → shifts left, K decreases. Endothermic+heat → shifts right, K increases. Only temperature changes K itself. Pressure/Volume: ↓volume → shifts toward fewer gas moles. ### Section 6: Common Ion Effect Adding a product-side ion already in the equilibrium shifts it backward, reducing solubility (e.g. NaCl reduces PbCl₂ solubility). --- ## 🎯 Clinical/Real-World Applications - Oxygen-hemoglobin binding is a real chemical equilibrium (Le Chatelier explains loading/unloading). - Blood pH buffering (bicarbonate system) is an equilibrium system. - Kidney stone formation is a solubility equilibrium problem. --- ## ⚠️ Common Mistakes - Thinking equilibrium means the reaction stopped. - Forgetting to omit solids/liquids from K. - Ignoring stoichiometric coefficients in ICE tables. - Confusing Q and K. - Assuming K changes with concentration/pressure (only temperature changes K). --- ## 📝 Quick Revision Summary - Equilibrium = forward rate = reverse rate. - Reverse → K becomes 1/K. Scale by n → K becomes Kⁿ. - Q\K shifts backward. - Only temperature changes K itself. --- ## ✅ Self-Test Checklist - [Remember] What does "at equilibrium" mean? - [Apply] Write a K expression, excluding solids/liquids. - [Apply] Calculate K for a reversed/scaled reaction. - [Apply] Solve an ICE table. - [Analyse] Use Q vs K to predict shift direction. - [Evaluate] Predict shift direction AND whether K changes for a given disturbance. --- Next: Electrochemistry →

resources.title: 05. Electrochemistry
resources.content: COURSE: CHM 101 \| LEVEL: 100L --- ## 📌 Learning Objectives 1. Distinguish strong from weak electrolytes, and cathode from anode. 2. Set up a galvanic cell diagram and calculate standard cell potential. 3. Apply the Nernst equation for non-standard conditions. 4. Use Faraday's laws for electrolysis calculations. --- ## 🔑 Key Concepts Two mirror-image ideas: galvanic cells (spontaneous reaction → electricity, i.e. batteries) and electrolytic cells (electricity → forces non-spontaneous reaction, i.e. electroplating). --- ## 📖 Detailed Notes ### Section 1: Electrolytes and Electrodes Strong electrolyte: >90% dissociated. Weak: partially dissociated. Cathode = reduction. Anode = oxidation. True in both cell types — only the charge SIGN flips between them. ### Section 2: The Galvanic Cell Daniell cell: Zn(s)→Zn²⁺+2e⁻ (anode), Cu²⁺+2e⁻→Cu(s) (cathode), connected by a salt bridge. Diagram convention: anode LEFT, cathode RIGHT — Zn/Zn²⁺(aq) // Cu²⁺(aq)/Cu ### Section 3: Electrode/Cell Potential Electrode potentials always tabulated as reduction potentials. SHE = 0V reference. E°cell = E°oxidation + E°reduction (oxidation value = negative of tabulated reduction value) ### Section 4: The Nernst Equation E = E° − (0.0591/z) log Ki (25°C, Ki = ionic product, not equilibrium constant) At equilibrium: E°cell = (0.0591/z) log Ke ### Section 5: Feasibility and Gibbs Free Energy Spontaneous → E°cell positive, ΔG negative. ΔG° = −zFE°cell ### Section 6: Electrolysis and Faraday's Laws Electrolysis = non-spontaneous, electricity→chemical (reverse of galvanic). | | Galvanic | Electrolytic | | --- | --- | --- | | Cathode charge | Positive | Negative | | Anode charge | Negative | Positive | | Spontaneity | Yes | No | Faraday's Law: m = (M × I × t)/(z × F) — time always in seconds. --- ## 🎯 Clinical/Real-World Applications - ECG/EEG measure the body's own electrochemical activity. - pH electrodes/meters work on electrode potential principles. - Pacemakers/insulin pumps run on galvanic cell chemistry. - "Electrolyte balance" (Na, K, Ca) is literally this chemistry, clinically. --- ## ⚠️ Common Mistakes - Mixing up cathode/anode charge sign between galvanic and electrolytic cells. - Forgetting to flip sign for oxidation potential. - Confusing Nernst's "Ki" with equilibrium constant K. - Time unit errors in Faraday's law (must be seconds). - Forgetting z changes per ion charge. --- ## 📝 Quick Revision Summary - Cathode=reduction, Anode=oxidation, always. - E°cell = E°ox + E°red. - ΔG° = −zFE°cell. - Faraday: m=(M×I×t)/(z×F), t in seconds. --- ## ✅ Self-Test Checklist - [Remember] Which electrode is cathode, which is anode? - [Apply] Calculate E°cell from two reduction potentials. - [Apply] Use the Nernst equation for non-standard concentrations. - [Understand] Why does positive E°cell mean spontaneous? - [Apply] Calculate mass deposited via Faraday's law. - [Analyse] Identify galvanic vs electrolytic and label charges. --- Next: Radiochemistry →

resources.title: 06. Radiochemistry
resources.content: COURSE: CHM 101 \| LEVEL: 100L --- ## 📌 Learning Objectives 1. Distinguish alpha, beta, gamma radiation by nature, charge, penetrating power. 2. Write and balance nuclear decay equations. 3. Apply half-life calculations, including non-integer half-lives. 4. Explain fission vs fusion; list clinical applications. --- ## 🔑 Key Concepts Nuclear reactions involve the nucleus, not just electrons. Three particles: alpha, beta, gamma. Decay follows first-order kinetics — same math as the Kinetics topic. --- ## 📖 Detailed Notes ### Section 1: Chemical vs Nuclear Reactions Nuclear reactions CAN convert elements, involve nucleus particles, are unaffected by temp/pressure/catalysts, release enormous energy. ### Section 2: Types of Radiation Alpha (⁴₂He): mass−4, charge−2. Beta⁻: neutron→proton+electron, atomic number +1. Beta⁺: proton→neutron+positron, atomic number −1. Gamma: no charge, EM radiation. Ionising power: alpha>beta>gamma. Penetrating power: gamma>beta>alpha (OPPOSITE order — most-tested fact). ### Section 3: Balancing Nuclear Equations Mass numbers balance both sides; atomic numbers (charges) balance both sides. ²⁰⁸₈₄Po → ⁴₂He + ²⁰⁴₈₂Pb ### Section 4: Half-Life t½ = 0.693/λ (independent of starting amount) Fraction remaining = (0.5)ⁿ, n = elapsed time ÷ t½ (works for non-integer n) ### Section 5: Fission and Fusion Fission: heavy nucleus splits, can chain-react (nuclear reactors). Fusion: light nuclei combine, releases MORE energy per unit mass than fission (powers stars). Both release energy via mass defect (E=mc²). ### Section 6: Detection Methods Geiger-Müller tube, scintillation counters, autoradiography, cloud chambers. --- ## 🎯 Clinical/Real-World Applications - Radiotherapy for cancer/tumor treatment. - Iodine-131 for thyroid/goitre treatment (uses half-life math for dosing). - Carbon dating. - Sterilizing surgical equipment. - PET/nuclear imaging. --- ## ⚠️ Common Mistakes - Mixing up ionising vs penetrating power order (they're opposite). - Confusing which decay type increases/decreases atomic number. - Forgetting half-life is independent of starting quantity. - Rounding non-integer half-lives incorrectly. --- ## 📝 Quick Revision Summary - Alpha: high ionising, low penetrating. Gamma: opposite. - β⁻ increases Z by 1; β⁺/K-capture decrease Z by 1. - t½=0.693/λ; Fraction=(0.5)ⁿ. - Fusion releases more energy per unit mass than fission. --- ## ✅ Self-Test Checklist - [Remember] State ionising/penetrating power order for alpha/beta/gamma. - [Apply] Balance a nuclear decay equation. - [Apply] Calculate fraction remaining after non-integer half-lives. - [Understand] Explain fission vs fusion. - [Analyse] Find a missing particle in a nuclear equation. - [Evaluate] Name 3 clinical applications of radioactivity. --- Next: Solutions & Solubility →

resources.title: 07. Solutions & Solubility
resources.content: COURSE: CHM 101 \| LEVEL: 100L --- ## 📌 Learning Objectives 1. Distinguish saturated, unsaturated, supersaturated solutions. 2. Explain ionic vs molecular dissolving; apply "like dissolves like." 3. Identify factors affecting rate of dissolving vs solubility itself. 4. Calculate molarity and prepare/dilute standard solutions. --- ## 🔑 Key Concepts Why does anything dissolve in anything else, and how much can dissolve? Two key ideas: "like dissolves like" and molarity. --- ## 📖 Detailed Notes ### Section 1: Vocabulary Solvent (dissolving medium), solute (dissolved substance), solution, aqueous solution. Miscible vs immiscible. ### Section 2: Saturation States Saturated = maxed out. Unsaturated = room for more. Supersaturated = unstable, over the max. ### Section 3: How Dissolving Happens Ionic (NaCl): ion-dipole hydration, ionic bonds break. Molecular (sugar): dipole-dipole, molecules stay intact, only intermolecular attractions break. Like dissolves like: polar/ionic dissolve polar/ionic; non-polar dissolves non-polar. ### Section 4: Electrolytes More ions in solution = stronger electrolyte (connects to Electrochemistry topic). ### Section 5: Rate of Dissolving Temperature, agitation, particle size — all increase RATE, not amount dissolved. ### Section 6: Solubility Itself - Nature of molecule (like dissolves like) - Temperature: SOLIDS ↑ with temp, GASES ↓ with temp (opposite trends!) - Pressure: only affects GASES (↑ pressure = ↑ gas solubility, Henry's Law) ### Section 7: Molarity M = n/V. Dilution: M₁V₁ = M₂V₂. Safety rule: always add acid TO water, never the reverse (exothermic hazard). --- ## 🎯 Clinical/Real-World Applications - IV fluids/injectables use precise M=n/V and dilution math. - Blood as a solution: Henry's Law explains gas exchange, diving medicine, altitude sickness. - Drug solubility affects absorption (pharmacology). - Kidney stones form via solubility limits. --- ## ⚠️ Common Mistakes - Assuming gas solubility behaves like solid solubility with temperature (opposite trends). - Forgetting pressure only matters for gases. - Confusing rate of dissolving with solubility itself. - Adding water to acid instead of acid to water. --- ## 📝 Quick Revision Summary - Saturated/unsaturated/supersaturated definitions. - Ionic = ion-dipole; molecular = dipole-dipole. - Solids ↑ solubility with temp; gases ↓ with temp. - Gas solubility ↑ with pressure (Henry's Law). - M=n/V; M₁V₁=M₂V₂; acid to water always. --- ## ✅ Self-Test Checklist - [Remember] Define saturated/unsaturated/supersaturated. - [Understand] Why do gas and solid solubility trend oppositely with temperature? - [Apply] Calculate molarity from mass and volume. - [Apply] Calculate dilution volume needed. - [Analyse] Predict solubility using "like dissolves like." - [Evaluate] Explain why the acid-to-water rule matters practically. --- CHM 101 Notes — Complete: Atomic Theory → Thermochemistry → Kinetics → Equilibria → Electrochemistry → Radiochemistry → Solutions & Solubility

resources.title: 01. Dimensional Analysis
resources.content: COURSE: PHY 101 \| LEVEL: 100L --- ## 📌 Learning Objectives 1. State the seven fundamental (base) quantities and their SI units. 2. Derive the dimensions of a derived physical quantity from base quantities. 3. Use dimensional analysis to check whether an equation is physically consistent. 4. Distinguish base units from derived units. --- ## 🔑 Key Concepts Every physical quantity in physics is built from a small set of fundamental (base) quantities — length, mass, time, and a few others. Dimensional analysis is the technique of tracking these base quantities through an equation, and it's one of the fastest ways to catch a wrong formula before you've even done the calculation. --- ## 📖 Detailed Notes ### Section 1: The Fundamental (Base) Quantities Physics recognizes seven fundamental quantities, each with a base SI unit and dimensional symbol: | Quantity | SI Unit | Dimension Symbol | | --- | --- | --- | | Length | metre (m) | L | | Mass | kilogram (kg) | M | | Time | second (s) | T | | Electric current | ampere (A) | I | | Temperature | kelvin (K) | Θ | | Amount of substance | mole (mol) | N | | Luminous intensity | candela (cd) | J | For 100-level mechanics, you'll mostly work with just L, M, and T. ### Section 2: Derived Quantities and Their Dimensions Every other physical quantity is derived by combining base quantities. To find a dimension, express the quantity's defining formula purely in terms of L, M, T. Velocity = distance/time → dimension = L/T (or LT⁻¹) Area = length × length → dimension = L² (LxL) Acceleration = velocity/time → dimension = LT⁻² Force = mass × acceleration → dimension = MLT⁻² Coefficient of linear expansion → dimension = Θ⁻¹ (per degree, since it's a fractional change per degree Celsius/Kelvin) ### Section 3: Using Dimensional Analysis to Check Equations A physically valid equation must have matching dimensions on both sides. This is one of the fastest sanity checks available — if the dimensions don't match, the equation is definitely wrong (though matching dimensions doesn't guarantee the equation is fully correct, since dimensionless constants can hide errors). Worked check: Is v² = u² + 2as dimensionally consistent? Left side: \[v²\] = (LT⁻¹)² = L²T⁻² Right side: \[u²\] = L²T⁻². \[2as\] = \[a\]\[s\] = (LT⁻²)(L) = L²T⁻² Both sides match — dimensionally consistent. ### Section 4: Base Units vs Derived Units A base unit (metre, kilogram, second, etc.) cannot be broken down further — it's a fundamental building block. A derived unit (newton, joule, pascal, etc.) is built by combining base units according to a quantity's dimensional formula. For example, the newton (force) = kg·m·s⁻², directly reflecting force's dimension of MLT⁻². --- ## 🎯 Clinical/Real-World Applications - Dosage calculations in medicine rely on unit consistency — the exact same discipline as dimensional analysis, just applied to mg/kg/hr instead of physics quantities. - Medical device calibration (infusion pumps, ventilators) depends on correct unit conversions, where a dimensional mismatch is a genuine patient-safety issue. - Any time you convert between unit systems (imperial to metric in older medical literature, for instance), dimensional consistency is the check that catches conversion errors before they become dosing errors. --- ## ⚠️ Common Mistakes - Confusing a quantity's unit with its dimension — units are the labels (metres, seconds), dimensions are the underlying physical nature (L, T) that the units measure. - Assuming dimensional consistency proves an equation is correct — it only proves the equation isn't obviously wrong. Dimensionless numerical constants (like the ½ in kinetic energy) can't be caught by dimensional analysis. - Forgetting that angles, and other dimensionless ratios, have no dimension at all (not even a special symbol) — they're pure numbers. --- ## 📝 Quick Revision Summary - 7 base quantities; for 100L mechanics, L, M, T matter most. - Dimensions are found by expressing a quantity's formula purely in base quantities. - Matching dimensions on both sides of an equation = necessary (but not sufficient) condition for correctness. - Base units can't be broken down further; derived units are built from them. --- ## ✅ Self-Test Checklist - [Remember] List the seven fundamental quantities and their SI units. - [Apply] Derive the dimension of force, area, and acceleration from their defining formulas. - [Apply] Check whether a given equation is dimensionally consistent. - [Understand] Explain why dimensional consistency doesn't guarantee an equation is fully correct. --- Next: Vector Analysis →

resources.title: 02. Vector Analysis
resources.content: COURSE: PHY 101 \| LEVEL: 100L --- ## 📌 Learning Objectives 1. Distinguish scalar from vector quantities with examples. 2. Add and subtract vectors, including using unit vector (i, j) notation. 3. Calculate the resultant of two perpendicular forces. 4. Compute the scalar (dot) and vector (cross) product of two vectors. --- ## 🔑 Key Concepts Not every physical quantity is fully described by a single number. Scalars need only magnitude (like temperature or distance). Vectors need both magnitude AND direction (like velocity or force) — and this distinction changes how you're allowed to add, subtract, and combine them. --- ## 📖 Detailed Notes ### Section 1: Scalars vs Vectors A scalar quantity has magnitude only — examples: distance, speed, temperature, mass, time. A vector quantity has both magnitude and direction — examples: displacement, velocity, force, momentum, acceleration. This distinction matters constantly: "distance" and "displacement" sound similar but distance is a scalar (just how much ground was covered) while displacement is a vector (straight-line distance AND direction from start to end point). ### Section 2: The Null (Zero) Vector A null vector is a vector whose magnitude is exactly zero. It has no defined direction, but it still behaves like a vector in calculations (e.g. the result of adding a vector to its own negative). ### Section 3: Unit Vector Notation and Vector Addition Vectors in a plane are often written using unit vectors i (x-direction) and j (y-direction). Adding vectors in this form is simple: add the i-components together, and add the j-components together, separately. Worked example: Given P = 5i − 2j, Q = 3i + 3j, R = 4i − j, find P + Q + R. ```javascript i-components: 5 + 3 + 4 = 12 j-components: -2 + 3 + (-1) = 0 P + Q + R = 12i + 0j = 12i ``` ### Section 4: Resultant of Perpendicular Forces When two forces act at right angles to each other, the resultant force is found using Pythagoras' theorem (since the two components form a right-angled triangle): Resultant = √(F₁² + F₂²) Worked example: A 40N force acts due East, a 30N force acts due North. Find the resultant. ```javascript Resultant = √(40² + 30²) = √(1600+900) = √2500 = 50N ``` Notice this is a 3-4-5 triangle scaled by 10 — a pattern worth recognizing quickly in exams. ### Section 5: Scalar (Dot) Product The scalar product of two vectors gives a scalar result: A·B = \|A\|\|B\|cosθ, where θ is the angle between them. Key fact: the scalar product of two vectors at right angles (90°) to each other is always zero — since cos(90°)=0. This is a fast way to test perpendicularity between two vectors. ### Section 6: Vector (Cross) Product The vector (cross) product of two vectors gives a NEW VECTOR result (not a scalar) — its magnitude is \|A\|\|B\|sinθ, and its direction is perpendicular to both original vectors (found using the right-hand rule). Key contrast to remember: dot product → scalar output. Cross product → vector output. This is the single fact most commonly tested about the two. --- ## 🎯 Clinical/Real-World Applications - Blood flow velocity in vessels is a vector quantity (magnitude AND direction matter for understanding circulation patterns and diagnosing flow abnormalities). - Force analysis in physiotherapy and biomechanics (how muscles and joints apply force at angles) relies directly on vector resolution and the perpendicular-force techniques covered here. - Any imaging technique involving directional fields (like MRI's magnetic field gradients) relies on vector mathematics at its core. --- ## ⚠️ Common Mistakes - Adding vector magnitudes directly without accounting for direction (e.g. assuming two perpendicular 40N and 30N forces simply add to 70N — they don't; Pythagoras applies instead, giving 50N). - Confusing the dot product (gives a scalar) with the cross product (gives a vector) — a very frequently tested distinction. - Forgetting that a null vector, despite having zero magnitude, is still technically a vector and behaves accordingly in vector equations. - Treating distance and displacement as interchangeable — distance is scalar, displacement is vector. --- ## 📝 Quick Revision Summary - Scalar = magnitude only. Vector = magnitude + direction. - Vector addition in i,j notation: add components separately. - Perpendicular force resultant: √(F₁²+F₂²) (Pythagoras). - Dot product → scalar result, zero when vectors are perpendicular. - Cross product → vector result, perpendicular to both original vectors. --- ## ✅ Self-Test Checklist - [Remember] Give three examples each of scalar and vector quantities. - [Apply] Add three vectors given in i,j notation. - [Apply] Find the resultant of two perpendicular forces. - [Understand] Explain why the dot product of perpendicular vectors is always zero. - [Analyse] Distinguish the dot product from the cross product in terms of their outputs. --- Next: Kinematics →

resources.title: 03. Kinematics
resources.content: COURSE: PHY 101 \| LEVEL: 100L --- ## 📌 Learning Objectives 1. Distinguish distance from displacement, and speed from velocity. 2. Interpret displacement-time and velocity-time graphs. 3. Apply the equations of uniformly accelerated motion to solve problems. 4. Explain the difference between average and instantaneous velocity. --- ## 🔑 Key Concepts Kinematics describes how things move — position, velocity, acceleration — without worrying about what causes the motion (that's the job of Laws of Mechanics, the next topic). Almost everything here builds from a handful of equations connecting displacement, velocity, acceleration, and time. --- ## 📖 Detailed Notes ### Section 1: Core Definitions Speed = distance/time (scalar). Velocity = displacement/time (vector) — direction matters. Average speed = total distance ÷ total time, regardless of the path taken. Instantaneous velocity is the velocity of a particle at one specific point along its path — not averaged over the whole journey. Worked example: A car travels 200km along a winding road in 2 hours. Average speed = 200/2 = 100 km/hr. Note this uses total distance, not straight-line displacement. ### Section 2: Graphical Interpretation The slope of a displacement-time graph gives velocity. If the slope is constant (a straight line), the object has uniform velocity. The slope of a velocity-time graph gives acceleration. ### Section 3: Equations of Uniformly Accelerated Motion Three core equations, all connecting initial velocity (u), final velocity (v), acceleration (a), time (t), and displacement (s): v = u + at s = ut + ½at² v² = u² + 2as Worked example: A body starts from rest (u=0) and accelerates uniformly at 5 m/s². Find its velocity after covering 90m. ```javascript v² = u² + 2as = 0 + 2(5)(90) = 900 v = 30 m/s ``` ### Section 4: Acceleration and Changing Motion When a body accelerates, its velocity is continuously changing — not necessarily its speed alone, but potentially its direction too. A common exam trap: an object CAN have constant speed while its velocity changes (moving in a circle at constant speed still has changing velocity, since direction is constantly changing) — this links directly into Circular Motion. A subtler trap: an object can have zero acceleration and still eventually reverse direction is FALSE — if acceleration is truly zero, velocity cannot change at all, so direction can never reverse without acceleration acting at some point. --- ## 🎯 Clinical/Real-World Applications - Gait analysis in physiotherapy relies on exactly this kinematic framework — position, velocity, and acceleration of joints during walking are measured using the same equations. - Ambulance response time calculations (distance, average speed, ETA) are a direct real-world kinematics application. - Understanding deceleration during a car crash (relevant to trauma medicine) uses the same v²=u²+2as equation, just solving for deceleration instead of final velocity. --- ## ⚠️ Common Mistakes - Confusing average speed (uses total distance) with average velocity (uses net displacement) — these give different answers on a winding path. - Assuming constant speed means constant velocity — direction changes (like circular motion) mean velocity is changing even at constant speed. - Forgetting units when using the equations of motion — always confirm consistent units (m, s, m/s) before substituting. - Believing zero acceleration allows eventual direction reversal — it doesn't; direction reversal requires acceleration at some point. --- ## 📝 Quick Revision Summary - Speed/distance = scalar. Velocity/displacement = vector. - Displacement-time graph slope = velocity. Velocity-time graph slope = acceleration. - v=u+at, s=ut+½at², v²=u²+2as — the three core kinematics equations. - Constant speed ≠ constant velocity if direction is changing. --- ## ✅ Self-Test Checklist - [Remember] State the three equations of uniformly accelerated motion. - [Understand] Explain the difference between average speed and average velocity. - [Apply] Given initial velocity, acceleration, and distance, find final velocity. - [Analyse] Explain why an object moving at constant speed in a circle still has changing velocity. --- Next: Projectile Motion →

resources.title: 04. Projectile Motion
resources.content: COURSE: PHY 101 \| LEVEL: 100L --- ## 📌 Learning Objectives 1. Describe the shape and key features of projectile motion (trajectory, range, time of flight). 2. Explain why projectile motion is treated as two-dimensional. 3. Analyse the vertical component of velocity at maximum height. 4. Calculate time of flight and range for a projectile. --- ## 🔑 Key Concepts Projectile motion is what happens when an object is launched and then moves under gravity alone. The trick that makes it manageable: split it into two independent, simultaneous motions — horizontal (constant velocity, no acceleration) and vertical (accelerating due to gravity) — and analyse each separately. --- ## 📖 Detailed Notes ### Section 1: Key Vocabulary The path followed by a projectile is called its trajectory. The range is the horizontal distance covered from launch to landing. Time of flight is the total time the projectile spends in the air. ### Section 2: Why Two Dimensions? Projectile motion is inherently two-dimensional — it has a horizontal component (constant velocity, since gravity doesn't act horizontally) and a vertical component (accelerating due to gravity, g≈9.8 m/s² downward). These two motions happen simultaneously but independently, and combining them produces the curved (parabolic) trajectory. ### Section 3: Behavior at Maximum Height At the very top of a projectile's path (maximum height), the vertical component of velocity is zero — the projectile momentarily stops rising before falling back down. The horizontal component of velocity, however, stays constant throughout the entire flight (assuming no air resistance). ### Section 4: Time of Flight Worked example: A ball is thrown vertically upward with initial velocity 50 m/s. Find total time in the air. Using v=u+at for the upward journey (v=0 at the top): 0 = 50 − (9.8)(t\_up), giving t\_up≈5.1s. Total flight time (up and back down) is double this: t≈10.2s (commonly rounded to \~10s in simplified problems using g=10 m/s² for cleaner numbers). --- ## 🎯 Clinical/Real-World Applications - Trajectory analysis is directly relevant to forensic/injury investigation — understanding a fall's height and impact speed uses projectile motion equations. - Sports medicine (analysing throwing/kicking biomechanics) often models limb or ball trajectories using exactly this two-component framework. --- ## ⚠️ Common Mistakes - Trying to analyse projectile motion as a single combined equation instead of splitting it into independent horizontal and vertical components. - Assuming horizontal velocity changes during flight — it doesn't (ignoring air resistance); only vertical velocity changes due to gravity. - Forgetting that at maximum height, vertical velocity is zero, but horizontal velocity is NOT zero (the object is still moving forward). --- ## 📝 Quick Revision Summary - Trajectory = path. Range = horizontal distance covered. Time of flight = total time in air. - Projectile motion = 2D: horizontal (constant velocity) + vertical (accelerating due to gravity). - At maximum height, vertical velocity = 0; horizontal velocity stays constant throughout. --- ## ✅ Self-Test Checklist - [Remember] Define trajectory, range, and time of flight. - [Understand] Explain why projectile motion is analysed as two independent dimensions. - [Apply] Given initial vertical velocity, calculate total time of flight. - [Analyse] Explain what happens to each velocity component at maximum height. --- Next: Circular Motion →

resources.title: 05. Circular Motion
resources.content: COURSE: PHY 101 \| LEVEL: 100L --- ## 📌 Learning Objectives 1. Explain why an object in circular motion is accelerating even at constant speed. 2. Distinguish centripetal from centrifugal force. 3. Explain the role of friction in circular motion (e.g. cars on roads). 4. Identify which quantities stay constant during uniform circular motion. --- ## 🔑 Key Concepts Circular motion is the classic case where speed can be constant while velocity is not — because direction is constantly changing. This constant change in direction means there's always an acceleration present, pointing toward the centre of the circle, even when speed itself never changes. --- ## 📖 Detailed Notes ### Section 1: What Stays Constant In uniform circular motion, speed and (for a fixed radius) the magnitude of acceleration stay constant. What does NOT stay constant is velocity's direction, and therefore velocity itself as a vector — it's continuously changing direction, pointing tangent to the circle at every instant. ### Section 2: Centripetal Force Centripetal force is the force directed toward the centre of a circular path that keeps an object moving in that circle rather than flying off in a straight line. Without it, an object in motion would simply travel in a straight line (Newton's First Law). ### Section 3: Friction's Role in Circular Motion For a car turning a corner, friction between the tyres and the road provides the centripetal force needed to keep the car moving along the curved path instead of skidding outward in a straight line. This is why icy or wet roads (low friction) make cornering dangerous — there isn't enough frictional force available to supply the needed centripetal force. ### Section 4: Centripetal vs Centrifugal Centripetal force is the real, physical force acting toward the centre (this is what actually acts on the object). Centrifugal force is not a real force in the traditional sense — it's the apparent outward force you feel in a rotating reference frame (like feeling pushed outward on a spinning ride), but from an outside, non-rotating viewpoint, it's really just the object's inertia resisting the curved path while the centripetal force pulls it inward. ### Section 5: Rotating Symmetrical Bodies A symmetrical body rotating about an axis, with one point fixed at its centre of gravity, is called a top (or more generally relates to gyroscopic motion — a spinning gyroscope maintains its orientation due to this same rotational principle). --- ## 🎯 Clinical/Real-World Applications - Centrifuges (used constantly in medical/lab settings to separate blood components) work directly on centripetal force principles — samples are forced into circular motion, and denser components settle outward due to their inertia resisting the curved path. - Understanding why vehicles skid on corners (friction limits) is directly relevant to trauma/emergency medicine's understanding of road traffic accident mechanics. --- ## ⚠️ Common Mistakes - Assuming constant speed in circular motion means no acceleration — there IS acceleration, because velocity's direction is constantly changing even though its magnitude (speed) is not. - Treating centrifugal force as a real, independent force acting on the object — it's better understood as an apparent effect of inertia in a rotating frame, not a true applied force like centripetal force. - Forgetting that friction is what supplies centripetal force for a car cornering on a flat road — without sufficient friction, the car cannot maintain the curved path. --- ## 📝 Quick Revision Summary - Constant speed ≠ zero acceleration in circular motion; direction constantly changes. - Centripetal force = real force toward the centre, keeps object on curved path. - Centrifugal force = apparent outward effect in a rotating frame, not a true independent force. - Friction supplies centripetal force for vehicles cornering on roads. --- ## ✅ Self-Test Checklist - [Understand] Explain why an object moving at constant speed in a circle is still accelerating. - [Remember] Define centripetal force. - [Analyse] Distinguish centripetal from centrifugal force. - [Apply] Explain the role friction plays when a car corners on a road. --- Next: Laws of Mechanics →

resources.title: 06. Laws of Mechanics
resources.content: COURSE: PHY 101 \| LEVEL: 100L --- ## 📌 Learning Objectives 1. State Newton's three laws of motion and apply them to solve problems. 2. Define momentum and impulse, and relate them via Newton's Second Law. 3. Distinguish elastic from inelastic collisions. 4. Apply conservation of momentum to solve collision problems. --- ## 🔑 Key Concepts This topic answers the question Kinematics deliberately avoided: what causes motion to change? Newton's three laws, plus the closely related ideas of momentum and impulse, form the foundation for essentially all of classical mechanics. --- ## 📖 Detailed Notes ### Section 1: Newton's Laws First Law (Inertia): An object stays at rest, or moving at constant velocity, unless acted on by a net external force. Second Law: The rate of change of momentum of a body is directly proportional to the applied force: F = ma (in its simplified form; more precisely, F = rate of change of momentum, F=Δp/Δt). Third Law: For every action, there's an equal and opposite reaction. ### Section 2: Momentum and Impulse Momentum (p) = mass × velocity, SI unit is kg·m/s (equivalently N·s). Impulse = force × time = change in momentum. This is why a longer contact/collision time reduces the force experienced for the same momentum change (the reasoning behind car airbags and crumple zones). Work is defined as force × distance (not force × time — that's impulse). Don't confuse the two. ### Section 3: Conservation of Momentum In a closed system with no external forces, total momentum before a collision equals total momentum after — this holds true regardless of whether the collision is elastic or inelastic. Worked example — Recoil velocity: A gun of mass M fires a bullet of mass m at exit velocity v. By conservation of momentum (initial momentum = 0 since everything starts at rest): ```javascript 0 = Mv(gun) + mv(bullet) v(gun) = −mv/M ``` The negative sign shows the gun recoils in the opposite direction to the bullet. ### Section 4: Elastic vs Inelastic Collisions Elastic collision: kinetic energy IS conserved (no energy lost to heat/sound/deformation) — momentum is also always conserved. Inelastic collision: kinetic energy is NOT conserved (some converts to heat, sound, or deformation), though momentum is still conserved. Perfectly inelastic collision: the colliding objects stick together and move as one afterward — kinetic energy loss is maximized in this case. Worked example — Perfectly inelastic collision: A 30,000kg truck at 10 m/s collides with a 1700kg car at 25 m/s moving in the opposite direction, and they stick together. ```javascript Taking truck's direction as positive: Total momentum before = (30000)(10) + (1700)(-25) = 300000 - 42500 = 257500 kg·m/s Combined mass = 31700 kg Final velocity = 257500/31700 ≈ 8.1 m/s in the direction of the truck's original motion ``` --- ## 🎯 Clinical/Real-World Applications - Understanding impulse (force×time = change in momentum) directly explains why airbags and crumple zones reduce injury — they extend collision time, reducing peak force on the body for the same change in momentum. This is core knowledge in trauma medicine and road safety. - CPR technique (force applied over the chest) and understanding impact forces in falls both draw on these same mechanics principles. - Ballistic pendulum-style momentum analysis is literally used in forensic medicine to estimate projectile speeds from injury/impact evidence. --- ## ⚠️ Common Mistakes - Confusing work (force×distance) with impulse (force×time) — these are different quantities entirely. - Assuming momentum is only conserved in elastic collisions — it's conserved in ALL collisions (elastic and inelastic); it's kinetic energy that's only conserved in elastic collisions specifically. - Forgetting to assign a direction (sign) to velocities in collision problems — momentum is a vector, so objects moving in opposite directions must have opposite signs in the calculation. - Mixing up which law explains what — First Law explains why objects resist changes in motion; Second Law quantifies how force causes change; Third Law explains paired reaction forces. --- ## 📝 Quick Revision Summary - Newton's 1st: inertia. 2nd: F=ma (rate of change of momentum). 3rd: action-reaction pairs. - Momentum = mass×velocity. Impulse = force×time = change in momentum. - Total momentum is ALWAYS conserved in a closed system, elastic or inelastic. - Elastic: KE conserved. Inelastic: KE not conserved. Perfectly inelastic: objects stick together. --- ## ✅ Self-Test Checklist - [Remember] State Newton's three laws of motion. - [Understand] Explain the difference between elastic and inelastic collisions. - [Apply] Given two colliding masses and velocities, calculate the resulting velocity for a perfectly inelastic collision. - [Analyse] Explain why a longer collision time reduces the force experienced during impact. --- PHY 101 Notes — Complete: Dimensional Analysis → Vector Analysis → Kinematics → Projectile Motion → Circular Motion → Laws of Mechanics
